chunks: "A reflection happens anywhere the impedance the wave sees changes, with a coefficient of load minus line over load plus line. So I walk down the path and list the changes.
At the ends: the driver, whose output impedance might be 10 or 20 ohms against a 50 ohm line, and the receiver, which is usually high impedance, near an open, so it reflects almost everything.

In the middle: stubs and T-junctions, because where a line splits in two the wave sees half the impedance; vias, which add some inductance and capacitance; pads and test points that add capacitance; width changes and neck-downs; layer changes where the reference changes; connectors; and any gap or slot in the reference plane, where capacitance drops and inductance rises.
Even bends and package bond wires add a little. To minimise them I first avoid the discontinuity: point-to-point routing, no stubs, fewer vias, constant width, solid plane.
Where I can't avoid it, I make it small compared with the edge: small pads, anti-pads under big pads, ground vias, shorter stubs.

And I terminate the line: a series resistor at the source so the driver plus resistor equals Z0, or a parallel terminator at the load, so whatever reflection remains gets absorbed instead of bouncing back and forth.
Then I check by simulation or TDR."
